reading.body:
Leticia Delgado is named on two Lobbying Disclosure Act filings about AI, filed through one lobbying firm for the AFL-CIO, and those filings name fifteen bills.

The pattern is concentration at the top and breadth below it. Two filings carry the disclosure, but the bill list runs to fifteen separate pieces of legislation, all dated 2025 or later. A single client relationship, the AFL-CIO, accounts for both filings. The firm is identified only by an internal identifier, so the data shows that a firm was used without saying which one.

For AI specifically, this is the legislative layer rather than the compute layer. Nothing here concerns data centers, power procurement, or interconnection queues. What it shows is that AI policy work is being routed through labor representation, and that the bills in play are numerous enough that no single statute defines the field. Anyone tracking AI regulation should expect the relevant text to be spread across many bills rather than consolidated in one.

What the data does not cover is equally important. It records that bills were named, not what they say, whether they moved, or what position the client took. It gives no dollar amounts, no agency contacts, and no outcomes. Two filings is a small base, and the page itself notes that a different lobbyist shares this name. The record establishes presence in AI lobbying, not influence over it.
